The train from Bologna to Florence takes about forty minutes if everything goes right. Nothing went right on that particular Tuesday in October.

I'd been in Italy for three days, running on espresso and stubbornness, dragging a suitcase with a broken wheel through cobblestone streets that were never designed for luggage. The trip was supposed to be relaxing — a solo getaway after months of grinding through a job I wasn't sure I even wanted anymore. Instead, I'd spent most of my time lost, sweating, and pretending to understand Italian beyond "grazie" and "un caffè, per favore."

The train was delayed. Of course it was. I sat on a metal bench in Bologna Centrale, watching pigeons fight over a discarded cornetto, and felt unexpectedly calm. There was nothing I could do. No email to send, no meeting to reschedule. Just waiting.

An elderly woman sat down next to me. She said something in Italian that I didn't understand, and I gave her my best apologetic shrug. She laughed and switched to English. "American?" she asked. "You look worried for no reason."

"I'm not worried," I said, which was almost true.

"Good. Worry is for people who think they control things." She unwrapped a sandwich from wax paper and offered me half. I took it because I was hungry and because saying no felt impossible.

We ate in comfortable silence. Her name was Giulia. She was going to Florence to visit her grandson. She'd made this trip hundreds of times and said the delays were the best part because they forced you to sit still.

The train finally came. I found a window seat and watched Tuscany unfold outside — rolling hills striped with vineyards, stone farmhouses sitting in pools of afternoon light, cypress trees standing like dark exclamation points against the sky. I'd seen pictures of this landscape a thousand times, but pictures don't capture the scale of it, or the way the light changes every few seconds as clouds drift overhead.

I arrived in Florence just before sunset. The city hit me all at once — the Duomo rising above everything, its marble facade turning pink in the fading light. I crossed the Ponte Vecchio with the crowd, gold shop windows glowing on both sides, and looked out at the Arno River. The water was the color of old copper.

I stood there for a long time, longer than I meant to. A street musician was playing something on an accordion that I almost recognized but couldn't name. Tourists bumped past me. The smell of leather and roasting chestnuts drifted from somewhere I couldn't see.

I didn't take a single photo. I just stood there.

Sometimes I think that's the moment the trip actually started — not when I boarded the plane, not when I checked into the hostel, but there on that bridge, eating a stranger's sandwich and watching a city I didn't know turn gold.

I went back to work the following Monday. But something had shifted, something small. I started paying attention to light again.
